edges.description: Neither substrate accumulated in brain or liver and the mice never developed organomegaly, so the storage step that defines human Gaucher disease is absent in this model despite the activator defect being present.
edges.limitations: This is a substantive negative result, not an unmeasured one: glucosylceramide and glucosylsphingosine were assayed in brain and liver of both genotypes and were not raised, and hepatosplenomegaly never appeared. The pathology that did develop - Purkinje cell loss, axonal spheroids, lipofuscin-like deposits - is a different lesion from lysosomal glucosylceramide storage, so this model cannot be used to study substrate accumulation, substrate-reduction therapy, or storage-burden endpoints. It remains informative for the activator defect itself (see the link above) and for axonal membrane homeostasis.

nodes.description: A homozygous C384S missense knock-in confined to the saposin C domain of prosaposin, plus a compound heterozygote over a null Psap allele (Psap<tm2.1Juma>, Psap(-/C384S)) that progresses faster. The design isolates loss of the activator from loss of the hydrolase: glucocerebrosidase itself is intact and present, and only its in vivo activation is impaired. The result is the reason this model is curated here - the mice develop progressive neurodegeneration without the glucosylceramide accumulation and organomegaly that define human Gaucher disease.

Saposin C arises from proteolytic cleavage of prosaposin (encoded by PSAP). Biallelic PSAP variants abolish saposin C, the activator protein that glucocerebrosidase requires to access and degrade glucosylceramide. Enzyme and GBA1 gene are normal; the defect is a missing activator cofactor.
